title: A detection overlay lets you check a measurement against the picture it came from
summary: Each overlay frame shows what the software decided is flame (green contour), where it put the centreline and tip, and the numbers it derived. Reading one means checking that the contour sits on the visible edge, that the tip marker is at the tip, and that the printed numbers are consistent with the picture and with one another.

media.alt: Portrait frame of a tall narrow white-yellow flame on a dark vertical burner tube, with a green contour tracing the flame edge, a thin orange centreline, a red cross at the tip and a blue vertical line through the burner axis. White text at the top reads Flickering Onset t = 317.28 s, length = 1456 px, max width = 161 px, area = 157342 px squared, rugosity = 1.04.

source.caption: Flickering-onset transition (detected contour overlay)
source.note: Four single frames of real footage with the measurement burned in: a green contour, an orange centreline, a red tip marker, a blue vertical reference line and a text block giving the regime label, the time and four numbers. They show the same pipeline on three regimes: ignition transient (MVI_8049, t = 5 s), flickering onset (MVI_8036, t = 317.28 s) and periodic flickering (MVI_8036 at 499.50 s and MVI_8041 at 339.34 s).

read_the_figure.question: Does the detected flame (contour, centreline, tip) match the flame in the picture, and what numbers does the pipeline derive from it?
read_the_figure.axes: There are no plot axes. The frame is a 1080 by 1920 pixel portrait image with the burner at the bottom centre. The text block gives the regime label, the time in seconds after ignition, and four quantities: length (px), max width (px), area (px squared) and rugosity (dimensionless).
look_at: Green contour: is it on the visible edge of the bright flame body, or does it hug the glow, include the faint halo, or miss the tip?
Orange centreline: it runs from the burner rim along the middle of the flame. In a bent flame (figures 12 and 20) it bends with the flame, and its length is longer than the straight tip height.
Red cross: the tip. Check that it sits at the top of the contour.
Blue vertical line: a fixed reference through the burner axis. Distance of the tip from it shows lateral displacement.
Text block: compare the label with the shape (a thin straight flame for onset, a bent kinked one for periodic flickering) and compare numbers between frames.
Figure 21: the ignition frame at t = 5.00 s is almost black. A faint spot near the burner is the first kernel; no contour or measurement text is drawn because there is no flame to measure yet.
read_the_figure.proves: A correct overlay shows that on this frame the segmentation found the flame and not something else, so that the numbers in the text block are measurements of the flame. One frame is an example, not proof: the claim needs many frames, including bad ones.
if_wrong: Contour larger than the bright body: a threshold set low enough to take in the halo, which inflates width and area.
Tip marker below or above the contour top: a tracking failure, usually from a detached or very faint tip.
Centreline that jumps or leaves the contour: a skeleton artefact on a kinked flame.
Printed numbers that are not consistent with what is visible: units or image size differ between the overlay and the displayed picture (see below).
must_check: Which pixel units the numbers use: they must refer to the same image size as the one displayed. Here the printed lengths are about twice the extents visible in the 1080 by 1920 frame, which suggests source pixels at twice the shown resolution.
The pixel scale (mm per pixel) is stated somewhere: none of these frames gives it.
The definitions of length, width and rugosity are given: they are not on the frames.
That frames from different regimes and runs are shown with the same overlay settings.
At least one failure case is shown, not only clean frames.
as_drawn: Printed values (overlay text), with ratios computed from them.
Figure 11, MVI_8036, flickering onset, t = 317.28 s: length 1456 px, max width 161 px, area 157342 px squared, rugosity 1.04. Length divided by width 9.0; area divided by length 108 px.
Figure 12, MVI_8036, periodic flickering, t = 499.50 s: length 1084 px, max width 186 px, area 173310 px squared, rugosity 1.05. Length divided by width 5.8; area divided by length 160 px.
Figure 20, MVI_8041, periodic flickering, t = 339.34 s: length 1416 px, max width 178 px, area 191302 px squared, rugosity 1.09. Length divided by width 8.0; area divided by length 135 px.
Figure 21, MVI_8049, ignition transient, t = 5.00 s: no measurement text; a single faint kernel.

terms.meaning: The closed outline of the pixels judged to be flame. Its area and perimeter come from it.
A curve through the middle of the flame from base to tip. Its length is the flame length when the flame is bent.
The brightness cut that separates flame from background. The contour moves outward as the threshold is lowered.
The largest horizontal width of the mask at any height.
The number of flame pixels, in pixels squared; multiply by the square of the pixel scale to get mm squared.
Length divided by max width: a thin flame is large, a stubby flame small.
A roughness ratio of the contour, near one for a smooth outline. The figure does not define it; a common definition is the contour perimeter divided by the perimeter of a smooth reference shape.
The first small luminous region of a flame, before it grows into an established flame.

remember: An overlay is an audit tool: the contour is a claim, the picture is the evidence.
Always check the units of the printed numbers against the size of the picture.
Convert pixels to millimetres with one factor, and squares of lengths with its square.
A lower brightness threshold makes the flame look larger.
One clean frame does not establish a method; failures need to be shown too.

understand.title: Why the contour is drawn on the frame
understand.text: If a number were reported on its own, the reader would need to trust the segmentation. Drawing the contour on the real frame shows exactly which pixels were counted, so a reader can see an over-large contour or a missed tip.

understand.title: What the three regimes look like
understand.text: Onset (figure 11) shows a tall thin nearly straight flame. Periodic flickering (figures 12 and 20) shows bent and kinked flames, shorter or longer than the onset frame depending on the phase of the cycle. The ignition frame (figure 21) is nearly dark, with a first luminous kernel.

understand.title: What the numbers say together
understand.text: Length and width differ strongly between the frames: length over width is 9.0, 5.8 and 8.0. The wide, shorter flame of figure 12 has area of 160 px per pixel of length against 108 px for the thin one of figure 11. The numbers separate shapes that the eye already separates.

understand.title: Why units matter here
understand.text: The printed length in figure 11 is 1456 px, but the flame in the 1080 by 1920 image is about 725 px tall. The factor is about two in all three overlays, so the numbers are probably in the pixels of the source video, which would be 2160 by 3840.

steps.title: Threshold the frame
steps.note: The mask M is 1 where brightness exceeds the threshold. The contour is the boundary of the largest connected region of ones. Otsu's method picks theta automatically from the histogram.

steps.title: Area and width from the mask
steps.note: Area is the count of flame pixels. Width at height y is the count of flame pixels in that row. The maximum over y is the max width printed on the frame.

steps.title: Flame length along the centreline
steps.note: For a bent flame the centreline is a curve c(u); its arc length is longer than the straight base-to-tip distance. The sum of segment lengths approximates the integral.

steps.title: Pixels to millimetres
steps.note: Lengths scale with s, areas with s squared. The same s must be used for the image whose pixels were counted: if the overlay counts source-video pixels, s refers to those.

steps.title: Effect of the threshold on the measurement
steps.note: Raising the brightness threshold shrinks the mask, so width and area fall; lowering it enlarges them. A measurement that depends strongly on the threshold has an uncertainty from that choice, which should be included in the error budget.

steps.title: Shape descriptors that compare frames
steps.note: The aspect ratio and the mean width area over length are dimensionless or scale-light ways to compare the three frames. They do not depend much on the unit of the pixels as long as both counts use the same unit.

worked.title: Compare the three flames from their printed numbers
worked.problem: Figure 11 prints length 1456 px, max width 161 px, area 157342 px squared. Figure 12 prints 1084, 186 and 173310. Figure 20 prints 1416, 178 and 191302. Compute the aspect ratio and the mean width for each.

solution.text: Aspect ratio, length divided by max width.
Mean width, area divided by length.

worked.answer: Figure 11 is the most slender (9.0, mean width 108 px), figure 12 the most compact (5.8, 160 px) and figure 20 in between (8.0, 135 px). All three mean widths are well below their max widths, as expected for a tapering flame.

analyze.q: The printed length in figure 12 (1084 px) is about twice the vertical extent you can see in the 1080 by 1920 image. What are two explanations, and which check would decide between them?
analyze.hint: Units of the overlay versus the displayed image, and a centreline that is longer than the straight distance.

analyze.q: Figure 20 shows an S-shaped flame. How does bending change the flame length measured along the centreline compared with the tip height above the burner?
Figure 21 has no measurement text. Why is it a legitimate frame of the pipeline's output, and what should the pipeline report for a frame like this?
analyze.hint: A flame must exist before it can be measured.

evaluate.q: Is showing three clean overlay frames enough to claim that the detector is reliable? What would you add?
evaluate.hint: Failure cases, a hand-measured check, threshold sensitivity.

evaluate.q: The overlay prints values in pixels only. Would you publish the figure like that?
evaluate.hint: Think of a reader who wants millimetres.

create: Redraw one overlay frame with a millimetre scale bar, the printed values in mm, and the threshold value used in the caption.
Design a four-panel failure-case figure for this detector: halo included, tip missed, detached fragment, and a bright reflection on the burner.

checks.q: What does the green contour claim?
checks.answer: That the pixels inside it are flame and the pixels outside it are not. Every number in the text block comes from those pixels, so a wrong contour means wrong numbers.

checks.q: A flame has length 1200 px and max width 150 px. What is its aspect ratio?
If the brightness threshold is lowered, what happens to the max width and the area?
checks.hint: The mask grows into the glow.
checks.answer: Both increase, because dimmer pixels in the halo are now counted as flame.

checks.q: An overlay prints a length of 1456 px, but the flame is 725 px tall in the image shown. Is the measurement wrong?
checks.hint: Which image are the pixels counted in?
checks.answer: Not necessarily. The numbers may be in source-video pixels (twice the shown size). It is wrong only if the scale used to convert to mm assumes a different pixel size from the one counted. State the pixel unit on the figure.

checks.q: How would you present a detector result so that a reader can trust it?
checks.answer: Show sampled frames with the overlay and a millimetre scale bar, state the threshold and pixel scale, include failure frames, and give the uncertainty from the threshold choice.

provenance.notes: Standard theory only. Numbers are the overlay text printed on the frames, plus ratios computed from them. Owner check: the printed length and width are about twice the vertical and horizontal pixel extents visible in the 1080 x 1920 images (for example length 1456 px against a visible flame about 725 px tall), so the overlay is probably in source-video pixels of a 2160 x 3840 frame; the page states this as an inference. 'Rugosity' is not defined on the figures; the page says only that it is a contour-roughness ratio near 1 and the owner should confirm the definition. Figure 21 (ignition transient) shows only a near-black frame with a faint kernel and no measurement text.
